evals.prompt: I maintain meshline-sdk, a TypeScript SDK on npm (currently 3.4.1, released with changesets). Last spring we wrote a SKILL.md for it and parked it with the skills for our two other libraries in bramwyn/agent-skills, since it was easier to review them together and that repo has its own release flow. Someone noticed the skill still shows metadata.version 3.2.0 even though it was accurate for 3.4.0 - we skipped the bump on the two patch releases because the skill text didn't change. The install line in our docs is `npx skills add bramwyn/agent-skills`. I want a plan to keep the skill aligned with meshline-sdk going forward, plus whatever CI check makes sense. Four-person team, keep it light.
evals.expected_output: A plan that moves the skill into the meshline-sdk repository, wires its version to the package version in the same release commit, pins every install command to a tag, and adds a version check plus a content check before any tag exists - each item audited against the lockstep rule.
expectations: Requires moving the meshline-sdk skill into the meshline-sdk repository itself, rejecting the shared bramwyn/agent-skills repo because a separate skills repo releases on its own clock and drifts by construction.
Requires metadata.version to equal the SDK version and to be bumped in the same commit or release job that bumps the package version.

Rejects skipping the bump on patch releases, stating the version is the lookup key and that 3.2.0 on a 3.4.1 tag reads as stale to every check; the bump happens by script and the content may stay identical.
Requires every release tag to carry a skill matching that tag's code.
Identifies `npx skills add bramwyn/agent-skills` with no ref as a default-branch install and replaces it with a tag-pinned form such as `npx skills add <owner>/meshline-sdk#v3.4.1`.
States that a release must fail before its tag exists when the skill is stale, rather than warn in a release log read after users installed the wrong skill.
Places the skill at skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md at the repository root.
Includes skills/ in the npm package files list so registry installs carry the skill, and checks the packed artifact contains it with `npm pack --dry-run`.
Wires the changesets version step to write the new package version into the skill and every manifest before the version PR merges.

Adds a content check beyond version equality - every symbol the skill names must exist and code blocks type-check with `tsc --noEmit` - stating that equal versions prove only that someone bumped a string.
Prints a tag-pinned install command in every release note, generated by the release job rather than typed by hand.
Audits the plan against the lockstep rule before anything else, instead of starting from the CI check the user asked for.

Asks the batched interview questions - release mechanism and version location, agent audience, three real agent failures, existing or community skills, deadline and effort ceiling - before finalizing.
Treats the skill name as public API: a later rename or removal is a breaking change of the SDK.

evals.prompt:
Here's the SKILL.md head we drafted for qn, our Go CLI (current release 2.3.0). Review it before I merge:

---
name: qn
version: 2.3
description: Helps with qn.
allowed-tools: Bash
compatibility: Requires qn >= 2.3.0 on PATH
---
# qn

Written for qn 2.3.x. If `qn --version` reports something older, tell the user to upgrade before continuing.

## Commands
qn deploy supports --env, --region, --timeout, --force, --no-verify, --legacy-auth
qn rollback supports --to, --dry-run
qn status supports --json, --watch

We also keep a copy of the full flag table in references/flags.md so agents don't need to run --help. Our repo is Apache-2.0.
evals.expected_output: A corrected frontmatter and body opening: version under metadata as a quoted string, no allowed-tools, unversioned compatibility, Apache-2.0 license, a what+when description, a two-sided Skill version guard in the body, and the flag dumps replaced by pointers to --help with job-shaped sections.
expectations: Moves version out of the top level into metadata.version as a quoted string, stating the Agent Skills spec has no top-level version field.
Removes allowed-tools because it pre-approves tools without a prompt.
Rewrites compatibility to declare the binary without a version number (for example 'Requires qn on PATH') so no second version string goes stale.
Sets license to the repository's own license, Apache-2.0, rather than defaulting to MIT.
Rewrites the description as what plus when, naming the tool and the tasks users type, instead of 'Helps with qn.'
Replaces the one-sided 'if older, upgrade' guard with a two-sided guard, because a silently upgraded binary passes a one-sided check.
Opens the body with a `Skill version: 2.3.0` line outside any code fence, because some harnesses never show the frontmatter to the model.

Specifies the guard branches: same major.minor continue; only the patch differs mention the matching tag once; major or minor differs in either direction trust `qn --help` over the skill's command names and tell the user to install the skill from their version's tag.
Specifies that a development build reporting `dev` continues.
Names no other version anywhere in the prose beyond that one body line.
Removes the pasted flag lists and the references/flags.md flag table, stating the tool owns WHAT (flags, arguments, defaults) and the skill points at `qn <command> --help` instead.
States the skill owns WHEN and WHY: which command for which job, ordering, safe defaults, and the real agent failures.
Restructures the body by job (for example 'Roll back a bad deploy') rather than by command group.
Keeps references/ for long-tail per-domain detail loaded only when needed, not for a flag dump.
Notes the bump script rewrites the Skill version body line and gate 2 checks it against metadata.version.

evals.prompt: We're Hollowmere; @hollowmere/ledger is our Node SDK, released through release-please (version lives in package.json). We ship a skill in-repo at skills/hollowmere-ledger plus plugin manifests for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini. Current release routine: release-please merges the release PR and creates the tag, then I run a small script that updates the version in SKILL.md and in the manifest files and push a follow-up commit. In marketplace.json I also set version on the plugin entry so marketplace users see the right number. Two users reported Claude Code says 'already latest' when they update, even after we shipped 2.6.0. What do we change?
evals.expected_output: A release-please configuration that bumps the skill and every manifest inside the release PR the tag points at, removes the post-tag follow-up commit and the marketplace entry version, and explains the 'already latest' symptom as a manifest version that never moved on the tag.
expectations: Identifies the post-tag follow-up commit as the defect: a bump made after tagging never reaches the tag, so every tag carries the previous version.
Makes package.json, the file release-please already bumps, the single source of truth and generates every other version field from it.
Adds each SKILL.md to release-please's extra-files as a generic updater entry (type generic, path skills/<name>/SKILL.md).
Annotates both version lines for the generic updater: `version: "x.y.z" # x-release-please-version` in the frontmatter and `Skill version: x.y.z <!-- x-release-please-version -->` in the body.
Lists each JSON manifest as a json extra-file with jsonpath $.version so the bump lands in the release PR the tag then points at.
Removes version from the marketplace.json plugins entry, stating plugin.json silently wins when both are set and the validator warns.
Explains 'already latest' as the installer keying its cache on the manifest version: a set but unbumped version reports already latest and users keep the stale copy.
Adds `git diff --exit-code` in CI after a fresh bump to catch a file the bump configuration forgot.
Runs scripts/check-skill-version.py with every --manifest on every pull request against the package.json version, and once more on the tag as a backstop.
Includes skills/ in the package files list and asserts `npm pack --dry-run 2>&1 | grep skills/` in CI.
Bumps on every release including prereleases, and runs the same bump and gates on maintenance branches.

Names all five manifest files at the repo root, each pointing at ./skills/: .claude-plugin/plugin.json, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, .codex-plugin/plugin.json, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json, gemini-extension.json.
Copies author, homepage, repository and license into the manifests from the existing package.json metadata rather than placeholder owners.
States that metadata.version is provenance for humans and guards; no installer reads it, installers resolve a git tag, a commit or a manifest version.

evals.prompt: Ferrisgate ships fgate, a Go CLI, with plain git tags and goreleaser (tag push triggers the release workflow, version comes from the tag via ldflags). We're adding skills/fgate/SKILL.md plus the plugin manifests. My idea: a goreleaser before.hooks step that rewrites the version into the skill and manifests from {{ .Version }}, then a content check that builds with `go build ./...` and runs `fgate deploy --help` for each flag the skill mentions, asserting exit code 0. Also, is it OK that our flags render as -yes in help? Users type --yes. Write the release wiring.
evals.expected_output: Release wiring where a make release target bumps and gates before the tag exists, goreleaser only verifies and packages, the content check builds an explicit stamped binary and compares flag names without dashes against stderr help output, and the tag-pinned install block lands in the release footer.
expectations: Rejects bumping in goreleaser before.hooks: goreleaser runs after the tag exists, so a bump there never reaches the tag.
Prescribes a `make release VERSION=x.y.z` target that runs scripts/check-skill-version.py with --write and every --manifest, then the gates, then commits, tags and pushes in one step.
Keeps before.hooks for gate 2 only, running the check (not the write) with {{ .Version }}.
Lists skills/** in goreleaser archives.files and asserts `tar tzf dist/*.tar.gz | grep SKILL.md`.
Puts the tag-pinned install block in goreleaser release.footer so the tag is never typed by hand.
Runs gate 2 on pull requests against `git describe --tags --abbrev=0` with fetch-depth 0, and again on the tag as a backstop, noting a tag-time failure means deleting the tag.

Rejects `go build ./...` for the content check: with several packages it writes no binary and the check silently runs whatever fgate is on PATH; requires an explicit `go build -o ./bin/fgate ./cmd/fgate` with the same -ldflags version stamping.
Recommends `goreleaser build --snapshot --clean --single-target` in a skill-gates job that the publishing job depends on.
Rejects asserting exit code 0 on --help, since some parsers exit 2 after printing help; asserts the output is help text rather than an unknown-command error.
Captures stderr (2>&1) because Go's standard flag package prints help to stderr, and compares flag names without leading dashes so -yes matches --yes.
Checks nested subcommands at every level, not only the first two tokens.
Adds the new-surface direction: diff the public command list against the last release and fail on an added command the skill never mentions and the allowlist does not exempt.
Suggests a hidden `commands --json` subcommand so extraction survives usage-layout changes.
Declares the tag as the version source of truth and records it with the tag format, gate list, channels and pinned-install command in memory when the harness has one.
Distinguishes the binary archive, which needs the explicit archives.files entry, from a Go module zip, which carries skills/ automatically for libraries.

evals.prompt: Nettlebrook here. Our Python CLI nb ships a skill in-repo and CI already fails a release if SKILL.md's version doesn't match pyproject. Last week a user filed an issue: the skill's migration section tells agents to run `nb sync --legacy`, which we removed in 3.0, and they'd been on 3.2 for two months - CI was green the whole time. Product now wants the fix to guarantee complete coverage: every nb command must appear in the skill, and the check should stop complaining about the --legacy mention since the skill deliberately says it was removed. Design the check.
evals.expected_output: A two-direction content check run on the release artifact: every named command and flag must exist, newly added public commands must be mentioned or allowlisted, intentional 'removed' mentions live in a small allowlist file, whole-surface coverage is refused, and a changed-surface gate covers pull requests.
expectations: States that version equality proves only that someone bumped a string and that lockstep rule 4 also requires the content check.
Runs the content check on the artifact the release will publish, built with the release version stamping, before any publish step.
Stale direction: extracts every invocation from fenced and inline code in skills/**/*.md and asserts every command, flag and identifier exists via `nb <subcommand path> --help 2>&1`.
Rejects the 'every command must appear' requirement: never require coverage of the whole surface, because it pushes the skill toward the command dump it should avoid.
New-surface direction: fails only on public commands added since the last release that the skill never mentions and the allowlist does not exempt.
Handles the deliberate --legacy mention with a small allowlist file next to the check, never by loosening the parser.
Fails on allowlist rot: an allowlisted 'removed' flag that exists again means the skill and the allowlist are both wrong.
Skips blocks marked as bad examples (lines under a ✗ label) during extraction.
When the skill names JSON fields to read, runs the command with --json against a fixture or dry-run and asserts each documented field is present.
Fails with the file, line and missing token.
Asserts the wheel's file list contains skills/.
Adds the changed-surface gate on pull requests: a public surface change with no file under skills/ changed fails unless a reviewer applies a skill-unaffected label.
Generates the surface snapshot with the head's script run against both the base and head builds, since the base may predate the script.
Proposes a hidden machine-readable command tree (`commands --json`) instead of parsing usage text that breaks on layout changes.

evals.prompt: I maintain verdant-orm, a TypeScript ORM on npm (v5). Agents keep generating repo.findOne() and the v3 Model.sync() pattern - both gone since v4. We shipped a SKILL.md in the repo three months ago and it names the new APIs, but the stale calls keep showing up in bug reports even from people who confirmed they installed the skill. Our users are all developers running Claude Code, Cursor or Codex in a terminal. Engineering's proposal is an MCP server that exposes the current schema and API surface so the model always has it. Six-week budget. Is that the right build?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the MCP server for a shell-equipped coding-agent audience, a diagnosis that always-needed API facts belong in bundled docs plus an agent-instructions pointer rather than an on-demand skill, the skill retained for workflows, and a library guard plus compile check on the skill's examples.
expectations: Rejects the MCP server for this audience: coding agents with a shell and the package installed locally get the skill plus bundled docs; MCP is promoted only for an audience without a shell.
Diagnoses the stale calls as the on-demand skill failing to trigger, citing the published eval where the skill was never invoked in 56% of runs while an always-loaded docs index scored 100%.

Classifies current API names and removed functions as knowledge every call needs, which belongs in docs bundled in the package plus a short pointer the tool writes into the user's project agent-instructions file.
Keeps the skill for multi-step workflows (setup, migrations, major upgrades) with references/, pointed at the bundled docs.
States the idle-context cost: a skill description costs about 100 tokens until it loads, while an MCP server's tool definitions typically cost one to two orders of magnitude more.

Ranks the add-beside options on separate axes - effort `MCP server > bundled docs + pointer > JSON output on the CLI > nothing`, value `JSON output on the CLI > bundled docs + pointer > MCP server > nothing`, efficiency `JSON output on the CLI > bundled docs + pointer > nothing > MCP server` - instead of one blended ordering.
Names the conditions that would promote MCP anyway (chat assistants or hosted fleets with no shell, hosted auth, remote state) and routes that design to the MCP sibling skill.

Opens the skill body with a library guard that reads the installed version from the project (node_modules/verdant-orm/package.json) rather than from memory, preferring bundled docs and type definitions when major or minor differs.

Adds a library content check: extract fenced TypeScript blocks from the skill and type-check them with `tsc --noEmit` against the release build, marking pseudo-code with a text fence the extractor skips.
Includes skills/ in the package files list so the skill ships inside the npm package, and notes the skills installer can link skills from installed dependencies so they update with the package.
Adds a runtime drift notice where the tool can know its version, printing one agent-parseable line on mismatch.
Asks for the three real agent failures as the skill's first content and tests, counting the findOne and Model.sync cases among them.

Names the skill after the tool and splits by job (verdant-orm, verdant-orm-migrations) only once SKILL.md passes about 250 lines, keeping the set small because large skill libraries shadow each other.
Uses the six-week budget as a standing-practice signal that promotes the starved bundled-docs rung, not the MCP server.

evals.prompt: Tarnwood monorepo: tw-cli (Go, currently 4.2.0, tags tw-cli-v4.2.0) and tw-sdk-js (TypeScript, 2.1.3, tags tw-sdk-js-v2.1.3), both released by release-please with component tags. We wrote a single skill at .claude/skills/tarnwood/SKILL.md covering both tools with metadata.version 4.2.0 since the CLI is the bigger one, and our root AGENTS.md already explains how to use both so maybe the skill can just point there. Teammates using Claude Code on the repo say the skill works great. Set up the versioning and the manifests.
evals.expected_output: Two user-facing skills under skills/, one per tool, each versioned against its own component tag prefix and shipped in its own artifact, with the repo-contributor skill directory and AGENTS.md left to their own audience and the manifests pointing at ./skills/.
expectations: Moves the skill out of .claude/skills/ into skills/<name>/SKILL.md at the repo root, stating .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/ serve agents working on the repo itself.
States the root AGENTS.md is contributor-facing and must not be mistaken for the user-facing skill: different audience, different file.
Splits into one skill per tool (tw-cli, tw-sdk-js), each checked against its own version and tag prefix, rejecting one skill carrying 4.2.0 for both.
Runs gate 2 with --tag-prefix tw-cli- and --tag-prefix tw-sdk-js- respectively, and triggers the tag workflow on *-v* tag patterns.
Wires each skill into release-please's per-component extra-files with the x-release-please-version annotation on both version lines.
Includes each skill in its own tool's release artifact: skills/ in the npm files list for tw-sdk-js, archives.files or embedded assets for the Go binary.
Explains the 'works great' report comes from teammates working inside the repo, the audience .claude/skills/ serves, not from users who install the tools.
Rejects 'the skill can just point at AGENTS.md': the user-facing skill carries its own WHEN and WHY and defers WHAT to `tw-cli --help` and the SDK's bundled types.
Shares cross-cutting rules (auth, output parsing) in one skill the others tell the agent to read first instead of copying them.
Keeps every skill harness-neutral: no harness-only frontmatter, no harness paths, capabilities described rather than tool names.
Points every plugin manifest's skills path at ./skills/ and keeps version out of the marketplace entry.
Treats each skill name as public API, so a later merge or rename ships in a major with a stub under the old name.
Asks which agents use each tool and what they get wrong today before writing content.

evals.prompt: Larkspur's CLI lark (Go, 1.8.0) is installed by almost everyone via Homebrew or our apt repo; a few use the GitHub release tarball. We added skills/lark/SKILL.md last month and the README says `npx skills add larkspur/lark` and `gh skill install larkspur/lark lark`. Three issues this week are agents using the skill's old `lark push` syntax after users upgraded to 1.8 via brew. Two-person team. What's the install story?
evals.expected_output: Tag-pinned install commands as the default, a README with a version placeholder, the install command printed from the binary for package-manager users, and - because most users arrive through Homebrew and apt - promotion of the bundled rung with an embedded skill, a skills install subcommand and a runtime drift notice.
expectations: Identifies the README commands as unpinned installs and switches the default rung to tag-pinned git installs.
Prints README commands with a v<your-installed-version> placeholder plus `lark --version` so the README never goes stale.

Generates the exact tag-pinned command per channel into every release note, naming at least `gh skill install larkspur/lark lark@v1.8.0`, `npx skills add larkspur/lark#v1.8.0`, `/plugin marketplace add larkspur/lark#v1.8.0` and `gemini extensions install ... --ref=v1.8.0`.

Explains the three issues: a tag-pinned install matches only at install time, and Homebrew upgraded the binary silently while the pinned skill stayed put, which is why the guard checks both directions.
Names binary-only package managers (Homebrew, apt, release download) as the promotion condition for the bundled rung: users get the binary and no skill, and skip the second manual step.
Prints the matching tag-pinned install command in `lark --help` or first-run output as the short-term fix.

Promotes the starved bundled rung because most users install through a package manager: embed skills/*/SKILL.md and skills/*/references with //go:embed from the module root and expose `lark skills install` or `lark update`.
Records the synced skill version in a small state file so the binary can detect drift.

Adds a runtime drift notice as one agent-parseable line (for example `skill lark 1.7.0 differs from lark 1.8.0; run: lark skills update`), skipped in CI and dev builds, with an environment variable to silence it.

Ranks the channels on separate axes - effort `bundled with the code > plugin marketplace pinned to a tag > tag-pinned git install > default-branch install`, with value and efficiency stated separately - and names bundled as the starved high-value option.
States unpinned `gh skill install` resolves the latest tagged release then default-branch HEAD, and that `gh skill update` skips pinned skills.

Notes `openclaw skills install git:` needs SKILL.md at the repo root so it does not fit skills/<name>/, and uses the bundle form `openclaw plugins install git:github.com/larkspur/lark@v1.8.0` instead.
Treats the README install section as the real driver of directory listings and adds the agent-skills repository topic.
Ends the release-note block with 'Already installed? Re-run with the new tag' or `lark skills update` once bundled.

evals.prompt: Moorhaven: moor CLI, Node, self-hosted Claude plugin marketplace in the repo (source "./"). Docs say `/plugin marketplace add moorhaven/moor`. We're about to cut 2.0.0-rc.1 from main - I'd keep the skill and manifests at 1.9.4 during the RC period since nothing is final, and tag it as a normal GitHub release so early adopters find it. I also submitted the plugin to the Claude directory last week; I left the branch field empty so it picks up whatever we merge. Our README is a 25-word tagline plus the install block. Anything to change before the RC?
evals.expected_output: Bump everything to 2.0.0-rc.1, cut the RC off the default install path and mark it a prerelease, move marketplace and directory tracking to a stable branch or release tag, and fix the README to clear the directory's word-count check.
expectations: Requires bumping the skill and manifests to 2.0.0-rc.1: bump on every release, prereleases included, because version equality is the contract.
Warns that a set-but-unbumped manifest version makes the plugin installer report 'already latest' so users keep the stale copy.
Cuts prereleases from a next branch (or tags a commit off the default branch) and keeps them off every default install.
Marks the GitHub release as a prerelease so latest-release resolution skips it, rejecting 'tag it as a normal release'.
Moves the stable branch or recommended marketplace tag only on final releases.
Explains that a self-hosted marketplace added from the default branch gives users merged-but-unreleased skill text under the last released version, and the cache may never refresh.
Changes the docs to add the marketplace at a release tag (`/plugin marketplace add moorhaven/moor#v1.9.4`) or at a stable branch moved only at release.

Sets the directory submission's 'Branch or tag' to the stable branch, stating that left empty it follows the default branch so every merge becomes a candidate version that goes live once auto-publish is on or someone selects Publish.
Notes a tracked tag in the directory must be re-pointed each release, which is why the stable branch is preferred.
Flags the README as blocking: the directory requires at least 40 words in the plugin folder README with code blocks not counted, plus a LICENSE file or license field.
Names the submission path: claude.ai/directory/manage on a paid plan, Submit new, Plugin bundle, the repository, then Validate.
Keeps the default branch releasable, or tells users a default-branch install may document unreleased features.
Mentions Gemini's --pre-release flag and that GitHub-Releases installs check the release marked Latest.
Runs gate 2 against 2.0.0-rc.1 on the release PR before tagging rather than only on the tag.

evals.prompt: Sedgebrook wants OpenClaw users covered for our sdg CLI (Apache-2.0, skills/sdg/SKILL.md, release 3.1.0). Plan: add metadata.openclaw: {"requires": {"bins": ["sdg"]}} to the frontmatter, drop an openclaw.plugin.json at the repo root so OpenClaw sees us, and publish to ClawHub from CI using ClawHub's reusable skill-publish.yml workflow. I also moved icon and documentationUrl into the marketplace.json entry so both files carry them. We're fine keeping Apache-2.0 on ClawHub. Check the plan.
evals.expected_output: A block-style metadata.openclaw gate admitted by the version check, no extra OpenClaw manifest, ClawHub publishing by direct CLI call with the release version, the MIT-0 relicensing stated plainly, and listing fields returned to plugin.json.
expectations: Rewrites metadata.openclaw in block style: OpenClaw reads it only as an object, a JSON string value is ignored, and strict YAML loaders including the spec's reference validator reject flow form.
Runs gate 2 with --allow-nested openclaw, admitting nesting only for that key because it is a spec deviation.
Sets requires.bins to sdg so OpenClaw offers the skill only where the binary is on PATH, and notes a sandboxed agent also needs the binary inside the container.
States no OpenClaw key gates on the tool's version, so the body's Skill version guard stays the only version check.
Rejects the root openclaw.plugin.json: it makes the repo a native plugin, and OpenClaw needs no extra manifest because it loads the repo as a bundle at a git tag from the existing manifests.
Names the detection order .codex-plugin/, .cursor-plugin/, .claude-plugin/ and therefore points every manifest's skills at ./skills/.
Rejects the reusable skill-publish.yml workflow because it has no version input; calls `clawhub skill publish ./skills/sdg --version 3.1.0 --owner <org>` directly in the release job.
Explains that without --version ClawHub starts at 1.0.0 and picks the next patch on each changed publish, which breaks lockstep rule 2.
Sets --categories (up to 3) and --topics (up to 5, with openclaw, clawhub, community and official reserved) once, since passing them publishes a new version even for unchanged files.
Warns that every ClawHub-published skill is released under MIT-0 whatever its license field says, so 'keeping Apache-2.0 on ClawHub' is not possible.
Notes a ClawHub release stays out of search and install until its security scan passes.
Moves icon and documentationUrl back to plugin.json only, because in a marketplace entry the validator reports the five listing fields as unknown.
Keeps OpenClaw's top-level extras (homepage, user-invocable, disable-model-invocation, command-* keys) out of the frontmatter, with metadata.openclaw.homepage covering the link.
Gives the tag-pinned OpenClaw install `openclaw plugins install git:github.com/<owner>/sdg@v3.1.0` and the ClawHub form with --version.
Points at `openclaw skills check` to debug a skill that installed but never appears, and notes a legacy metadata.clawdbot block is ignored.

evals.prompt: Pellmoor pell CLI. Our skill ships scripts/refresh-docs.sh which curls https://docs.pellmoor.dev/agents/latest.md at run time, and the SKILL.md tells the agent to read it and follow the steps there, so the skill never goes stale. For the security gate I drafted: a job on pull_request_target (so fork PRs get scanned too) running `uvx snyk-agent-scan@latest --ci --dangerously-run-mcp-servers --skills ./skills` with SNYK_TOKEN: <our token> in the env block, then a step that parses the JSON report and fails if prompt_injection appears. Our repo is private for now. Review it.
evals.expected_output: Removal of the fetch-and-follow mechanism in favour of lockstep shipping, and a corrected scan job: token from secrets, no pull_request_target with the MCP flag, fork PRs skipped, pinned scanner and setup-uv versions, exit-code gating, and the private-repo upload cleared.
expectations: Removes the fetch-and-follow instruction and script: telling the agent to fetch and follow remote content is the most common audit finding on benign skills and an indirect-injection exposure.
Replaces it with the lockstep approach: the skill stays current by shipping in the repo at every tag, not by fetching at run time.
States that when fetching is the tool's purpose, fetched content must be marked as data never instructions, and only then `--ignore-risks third_party_content_exposure` with the reason in a comment.
Requires SNYK_TOKEN to come from a repository or organization secret, never written inline.
Rejects running the scan with --dangerously-run-mcp-servers on pull_request_target from forks, because that flag starts and contacts every MCP server the scanned configs declare.
Explains fork pull requests get no secrets so the scan fails there; skips the step with `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` and relies on the release-job run.
Keeps --dangerously-run-mcp-servers because --ci requires it, noting that with only ./skills as target it starts nothing.
Gates on the exit code, never on parsed output, because the scanner's output and risk names change between releases.
Pins the scanner version (replaces @latest with @<version>) so release gates stay reproducible.
Adds astral-sh/setup-uv pinned to a commit SHA because ubuntu-latest ships no uv and the action publishes no major-version tag.
Flags that the scan uploads skill content to Snyk, which must be cleared for the private repo.
Keeps scripts/ few, readable, offline and dependency-pinned, calling the tool's own published CLI rather than bundling binaries.
States a clean scan is a floor, never a trust claim, because admission scanners are evadable.
Runs the scan on skills/** changes in pull requests and in the release job next to the pinned spec validator, and signs release tags.

evals.prompt: Oakenshaw's oak CLI skill went live two releases ago. For the next planning review I want to show it's working: we're at 2,300 installs on skills.sh and climbing, so I'd headline that. For CI, I want to start with an agent-in-the-loop suite as the first gate before we bother with the cheaper checks - run 20 real tasks through Claude Code with the skill on every PR and block merges when the pass rate drops at all. One more thing: the suite shows the skill only gets loaded in about a third of runs, so I'm planning to rewrite most of the body. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Correctness metrics replacing the install count, the default gate rung installed before any golden suite, a right-sized golden suite that reports rather than blocks until stable, and the low trigger rate attributed to the description or to always-loaded docs rather than the body.
expectations: Refuses the install count as the headline: install counts measure interest and can be inflated; measure correctness, not reach.
Names the signals that matter: trigger and pass rate per release, issues tagged 'agent misuse', and how often the drift notice fires.
Notes skills.sh ranks by installs reported by the installer's telemetry and that the README install section is the listing's real driver, separating listing from correctness.
Rejects golden agent tasks as the first gate: they are the highest-effort, starved gate; promote them once agents are a main user channel or after the first issue traced to a wrong skill.
Prescribes the default rung instead: gates 1-3 and 6 before tagging, gates 1-4 and 6 on pull requests.

Ranks the gates on separate axes - effort `golden agent tasks > content check > changed-surface check > version equality == spec validation == security scan`, value `content check > golden agent tasks > version equality > changed-surface check > security scan > spec validation`, efficiency `version equality == spec validation > content check > security scan > changed-surface check > golden agent tasks` - and justifies the version-equality/spec-validation tie as two one-command offline checks catching different failures.
Sizes the golden suite at 3-10 tasks drawn from real agent failures, each with a binary pass condition (exit code, file produced, test passing), not 20.
Runs each task with and without the skill on a pinned agent and model against the built tool, recording two numbers: trigger rate and pass rate.
Rejects blocking on any drop: a drop is a release blocker only once the suite is stable; until then report it, and run the suite optional or nightly on pull requests.
Diagnoses the one-third trigger rate as a description problem, or a sign the knowledge belongs in always-loaded bundled docs, not a body-content problem - rejecting the body rewrite.
Sets expectations that published benchmarks show skills help least on software-engineering tasks, so gains are small and noisy and judged on the project's own tasks.

States the four pass conditions of the setup: a deliberately stale metadata.version fails before its tag exists, a skill naming a removed flag fails CI, every manifest version equals the tag on the last three releases, every release note prints a tag-pinned install command.
Adds repository topics directory crawlers index (agent-skills, gemini-cli-extension) and links the install command from the official docs.

evals.prompt: Thornquist: TypeScript CLI thorn, repo root holds package.json plus package-lock.json, about 1,400 files, docs/ has a 3 MB architecture PNG and a 600 KB PDF, a README.md -> docs/README.md symlink, .gitattributes with `tests/ export-ignore`, and a helper script that runs `npx prettier`. plugin.json sits at the root. The Claude directory validation came back 'Couldn't validate that repository' with nothing else. Separately, we want to rename the skill from thorn to thornquist-cli in next week's 2.4.1 patch. Get us through validation and the rename.
evals.expected_output: The export-ignore and symlink identified as the silent validation failures, the reviewer holds listed with the plugin moved into a subfolder to escape the root lockfile cost, launchers pinned, and the rename deferred to a major release with a stub skill and a renames entry.
expectations: Identifies the .gitattributes export-ignore as a cause of 'Couldn't validate that repository': no export-ignore or export-subst in any .gitattributes, and no content filter (Git LFS included) at, above or inside the plugin folder.
Identifies the README symlink as blocking: no symlinks, submodules or LFS pointers for loaded files.

Checks file names valid on Windows and macOS (no colon, trailing dot or space, device names, case-only twins) and plugin-path folders limited to letters, digits, dot, hyphen and underscore, as the other causes that report only that message.
Pins the npx prettier launcher to an exact version and checks there is no .npmrc, bunfig.toml or uv.toml setting a registry beside one.
Lists the reviewer holds the repo will hit: more than 512 files, the 600 KB PDF as a non-image file over 256 KiB, binary files, and the root package.json with a lockfile.
Explains the root lockfile makes Claude Code install the tool's npm dependencies into the plugin cache on every install and update.
Moves the plugin to a subfolder that holds skills/ itself, then repoints every manifest's skills path and gate 2's --skills-dir, noting a component path outside the plugin folder blocks.
Checks the 3 MB PNG against the 5 MiB per-file limit and the repo against 50 MiB archived, 256 MiB unpacked and 10,000 entries.
Requires a README of at least 40 words in the plugin folder, code blocks not counted, and a LICENSE file or license field.
Rejects the rename in a 2.4.1 patch: a skill rename is a breaking change of the tool and ships in a major release.
Keeps a stub skill under the old name thorn for one major that points at thornquist-cli.
Adds an entry to the marketplace renames map as a supplement, never as the only signal.
Notes spec validation fails when the skill name does not match its directory, so the directory renames with it.
Checks for .DS_Store, Thumbs.db, desktop.ini or __MACOSX entries in the plugin folder.

evals.prompt: I maintain rushmere, a Python data-validation library on PyPI (version in pyproject.toml, released by a tag-push workflow with trusted publishing). Agents keep calling rushmere.validate(schema, data) with the arguments swapped, importing rushmere.legacy which we deleted in 2.0, and setting strict=False by default which hides errors. I need a skill shipped by Friday, I've got one afternoon. There's already a community SKILL.md for rushmere on skills.sh under someone else's account that's pretty wrong. Just tell me what to do.
evals.expected_output: A one-afternoon plan on the default rungs: interview batched up front, the three failures as first content and tests, the skill under skills/ shipped in the wheel, pyproject as the version source with the gate on PRs and tags, compile checks on examples, the community skill answered by owning the namespace, and the starved rungs deferred.
expectations: Batches the interview questions before designing: agent audience, release mechanism and license, existing skills including the community one, deadline and effort ceiling, and whether the package may gain a console command.
Keeps the default rungs because of the near deadline, deferring the starved options (bundled install command, golden agent tasks).
Turns the three named failures (swapped arguments, rushmere.legacy import, strict=False) into the skill's first content and its tests.
Places the skill at skills/rushmere/SKILL.md at the repo root and includes skills/ as package data so the wheel carries it.
Makes pyproject.toml the version source of truth, bumps metadata.version and the Skill version body line in the release commit, and adds a check that the tag equals the pyproject version.
Runs scripts/check-skill-version.py on pull requests against the pyproject version and on the tag as a backstop.
Adds the library content check: `python -m py_compile` plus an import smoke test on every extracted code block against the release build.
Opens the body with a library guard that reads the installed version (`pip show rushmere`) and prefers bundled docs when major or minor differs.
Handles the community skill by publishing under the project's own namespace and claiming obvious name variants, because agents hallucinate skill names and attackers register them.
Sets license to the repo's license and writes the description as what plus when, with the tool's name and the tasks users type.
Delivers the expected output shape: repo layout, version-wiring change, CI gate list with commands, install commands per channel and manifests, each checked against the lockstep rule.
Records the version source of truth, tag format, gate list, chosen channels and pinned-install command in memory when the harness has one.
Pins the spec validator (skills-ref, an alpha requiring Python 3.11+) by version in CI rather than installing it unpinned.

evals.prompt: Inglewick ing CLI: we develop on main, release every two weeks, skill in the repo, five manifests all bumped by our release script. A curated community marketplace lists us with a sha they set three months ago and haven't touched. Cursor users say they're seeing unreleased commands in the skill; Codex users say they're stuck on an old copy. One suggestion internally is to stop bumping the Cursor manifest since Cursor ignores versions anyway. What do we tell each group of users and what do we change?
evals.expected_output: Per-channel explanations grounded in how each installer resolves a ref, one of the two default-branch fixes chosen, every manifest kept bumped from one source, the curator's sha accepted as the pinning model, and tag-pinned commands for every channel in the release notes.
expectations: Explains Cursor users get unreleased text because Cursor plugins follow git commits rather than the manifest version, and a default-branch install documents unreleased features.

Offers the two fixes and picks one: keep the default branch equal to the latest release with development on a dev branch merged at release time, or keep development on main and print the tag-pinned command everywhere users copy install commands.
Rejects stopping the Cursor manifest bump: bump every plugin manifest from one source on every release and never leave one manifest set but unbumped (the mixed-manifest trap).
Explains curated marketplaces pin exact commits, expects the curator to bump the sha, and makes each tag's commit the one worth pinning rather than asking for a tracking ref.
States Codex installs use --ref defaulting to main, so users re-install at the new ref; gives the tag-pinned form.

Gives per-channel tag-pinned commands: `gh skill install`, `npx skills add <owner>/ing#v<tag>`, `/plugin marketplace add <owner>/ing#v<tag>`, `gemini extensions install ... --ref=v<tag>`, `openclaw plugins install git:...@v<tag>`.
Notes `gh skill install` writes repo, ref, pin and tree SHA into the installed SKILL.md frontmatter, and `gh skill update` skips pinned skills.
Notes the skills installer's skills-lock.json records the ref and a content hash, and that a branch ref floats while a tag or SHA holds.
States a tag-pinned install matches only at install time and the binary can upgrade silently, so the body guard checks both directions.
Mentions a stable branch moved only at release as the alternative to a tag for marketplace and directory tracking.
States the Claude Code plugin version resolves from plugin.json version, else the marketplace entry, else the commit SHA, and keeps it bumped so update does not report 'already latest'.
Generates the release-note install block in the release job so the tag is never typed by hand, ending with 'Already installed? Re-run with the new tag (OpenClaw: add --force)'.
States that no installer resolves 'the skill matching the code I installed' by itself.
